lesson.title: The Loop Body: What Actually Happens Each Time Around
lesson.summary: The loop body is the indented block of statements beneath a for or while header that runs once per iteration, and it is where a loop's real work, and its most common bugs, actually live.
lesson.body:
A loop header, whether it starts with for or while, only sets up the repetition; it does not do any actual work by itself. The real work happens in the loop body: the indented block of statements underneath the header, which Python runs from top to bottom, in full, on every single pass through the loop. In that sense, a loop body is nothing exotic, it is simply a sequence of ordinary statements, the same kind you would write outside a loop, just packaged so the whole group repeats together as one unit.

Because the body is just statements, it can contain anything statements can: variable assignments, function calls, print statements, if-else branches, and even other loops nested inside it. There is no fixed limit on how many lines the body holds, only that every line inside it must share the same indentation level, which is precisely how Python knows a given line belongs to the loop rather than to whatever code follows it.

Here is a loop body doing several things per pass, not just one:
total = 0
for number in [4, 7, 2]:
    doubled = number * 2
    total += doubled
    print(doubled)
Trace through all three statements on each pass. First pass: number is 4, doubled becomes 8, total becomes 0 + 8 = 8, and 8 is printed. Second pass: number is 7, doubled becomes 14, total becomes 8 + 14 = 22, and 14 is printed. Third pass: number is 2, doubled becomes 4, total becomes 22 + 4 = 26, and 4 is printed. After the loop finishes, total holds 26, even though no code after the loop mentions doubled at all, because doubled was effectively recreated fresh on each pass, useful only for that pass's work.

Indentation is not just a style preference here, it is what defines the body's boundaries in the first place. Python typically uses four spaces per indentation level, and every statement meant to run with each repetition must be indented consistently at that level. A line that is accidentally indented one level too little falls outside the loop and only runs once, after the loop finishes entirely, rather than repeating along with everything else; this is one of the most common early bugs when learning loops, and it is always worth double-checking indentation carefully whenever a loop behaves unexpectedly. Mixing tabs and spaces within the same body can produce the same kind of confusing failure, which is why most style guides insist on spaces only.

Ultimately, the loop body is where the general idea of statements meets the general idea of loops: it takes ordinary sequential code, the kind you already know how to write and reason about, and wraps it in repetition, so the same set of instructions becomes useful across many passes instead of running just once and being done. Learning to read a loop body correctly, tracing each statement in order and updating your mental picture of every variable after each line, is the single most reliable way to predict what any loop, however unfamiliar, will actually do when it runs.
